content: Low back pain is recognized as a significant global public health issue. Currently, there is no comprehensive international guideline that addresses the management of low back pain (LBP) while considering the needs of older adults and the diverse healthcare contexts across different countries. This gap highlights the importance of developing such a guideline at this time. The World Health Organization (WHO) has introduced a guideline for the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults, specifically designed for use in primary and community care settings. This initiative, led by Dr. Andrew Briggs from the Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child & Adolescent Health & Ageing at WHO, aims to address the growing burden of chronic low back pain. Chronic pain, including low back pain, has far-reaching consequences for individuals, families, communities, and healthcare systems. Despite advancements in treatment, the prevalence of low back pain, associated disability, and healthcare costs continue to rise. Challenges such as unwarranted variations in care, gaps in knowledge and skills among healthcare providers, and the persistence of non-evidence-based practices remain significant barriers to effective management. The guideline emphasizes the importance of conducting a thorough clinical assessment of low back pain from a biopsychosocial perspective. It recommends providing personalized, rather than generic, information and advice to help individuals understand their pain and re-engage in meaningful activities. For some patients, a comprehensive package of care may be more beneficial than isolated interventions. The development of this guideline involved contributions from an external review group, including experts such as Hanadi Khamis Alhamad, Cyrus Cooper, Pierre Côté, Helen Foster, Janet Gunderson, Scott Haldeman, Jaro Karppinen, Bart Koes, Andrew McLachlan, Seiji Okada, Livia Puljak, François Rannou, Robyn Speerin, and Steven Vogel. Systematic review teams and methodologists, led by Nandi Siegfried, and editorial oversight by Iain Bamforth, also played key roles in the process. The guideline was supported by funding from the governments of Canada, Germany, and Japan, as well as the Kanagawa Prefectural Government in Japan. This collaborative effort aims to provide evidence-based, context-sensitive recommendations to improve the management of chronic low back pain globally.
